<objective>
Give a resume somewhere to live: two nullable columns, a shipped migration, and a service function that
decides — with named errors — whether a given task may be continued at all.

Purpose: RUN-06 is the phase's third built-but-unwired primitive. `buildSpawnArgv()` has correctly emitted
`--resume <id> --fork-session` since plan `02-06` and is unit-tested doing so, and nothing in production has
ever called it. Closing it needs a place for the session id to be read back from at dispatch time, because
`Scheduler.dispatch()` builds its `RunnerTask` from the task row and nothing else — a value handed over
in-memory at request time would not survive the daemon restart that a queued task can legitimately outlive.

The load-bearing decision is not the columns, it is what a resume IS. `src/core/state-machine/transitions.ts`
states, in its own doc comment, that `failed` and `rejected` are fully terminal and that "retrying a failed
or rejected task means creating a new task row, never transitioning this one back" — that is D-06, and it is
the property that keeps the state graph a DAG. A resume that reopens the original contradicts it directly.
Task 1 puts that choice in front of a human before any of it is built, because it is baked into both the
state graph and a published CLI and HTTP contract once shipped.

Output: a decided resume semantics, two nullable columns with a real generated migration, and a validation
function that refuses every way a resume can be meaningless — including the one nobody asks about, an
unbounded chain of continuations quietly walking down a subscription window.
</objective>

<task type="checkpoint:decision" gate="blocking">
  <name>Task 1: Decide what a resume is — a new task row, or a reopened one</name>
  <decision>
Does `fleet task resume <id>` create a NEW task row that continues the original's session, or does it move
the ORIGINAL task row back into `running`?
  </decision>
  <context>
RUN-06 says sessions can be continued via `--resume` with the stored session id. It does not say what
happens to the task row, and the two available answers pull against two different things this phase already
locked.

`src/core/state-machine/transitions.ts` is explicit in its own doc comment: `failed` and `rejected` are
fully terminal, both are empty rows in the transition table, and "retrying a failed or rejected task means
creating a new task row, never transitioning this one back to `queued` — that keeps the state graph a DAG
and each task's event log a single unambiguous story." That is D-06. Every Phase 2 non-success exit —
timeout, crash, cancel, rate-limit — lands in `failed`, so `failed` is the state a resumable task is
overwhelmingly in.

Pulling the other way, `02-CONTEXT.md` D-16 says a resume "re-spawns in the same worktree". That phrasing
predates the reality D-23 created: archival fires immediately on transition to a terminal state, removing
the working directory and deliberately keeping the branch ref. So the same worktree does not exist by the
time anyone resumes; the branch does, precisely so the work survives.

This is being asked now rather than assumed because it is one-way in practice. The answer is baked into the
state graph, into what the new endpoint returns, and into what `fleet task resume` prints. Reversing it later
means adding an edge out of a state the transition table declares terminal, and changing what a shipped
command returns.
  </context>
  <options>
    <option id="fork-new-row">
      <name>Fork a new task row (recommended)</name>
      <pros>
Honours D-06 exactly as `transitions.ts` states it — no edge out of a terminal state, the graph stays a DAG,
and each task's event log stays one unambiguous story. Honours the project's `one task -> one branch -> one
worktree -> one agent` constraint: the resumed task gets its own branch, cut from the parent's surviving
branch tip, so the prior work is present and the review unit stays one branch per task. Reuses the existing
dispatch path wholesale — concurrency cap, kill switch, worktree locking and archival all apply with no
special case. Lineage is explicit and queryable rather than implied by a status that moved backwards.
      </pros>
      <cons>
`fleet task resume <id>` prints a DIFFERENT id than the one you passed it, which is mildly surprising the
first time. Two rows exist for what an operator may think of as one piece of work, so "what happened to that
task" becomes a chain walk rather than a single lookup. Costs two nullable columns and a migration.
      </cons>
    </option>
    <option id="reopen-original">
      <name>Reopen the original task row</name>
      <pros>
One row per piece of work; the id you pass is the id you keep watching. No new columns and no migration.
Matches the naive mental model of the word "resume".
      </pros>
      <cons>
Requires adding a transition out of `failed`, directly contradicting D-06 and the transition table's own
stated rationale. The event log for that task becomes a cycle, so "why did this task fail" no longer has one
answer. The worktree was already archived on the way into `failed` (D-23), so re-provisioning has to
special-case a state that the terminal path assumed it would never leave. Every consumer that treats a
terminal state as final — including future crash reconciliation in Phase 4 — inherits a new case.
      </cons>
    </option>
  </options>
  <reversibility rating="one-way">The choice is encoded in the state graph's acyclicity and in what a published CLI command and HTTP route return. Reversing it means adding an edge out of a state the transition table declares terminal and changing a shipped contract's return value.</reversibility>
  <resume-signal>Select: fork-new-row, or reopen-original. If fork-new-row, Tasks 2 and 3 proceed as written. If reopen-original, STOP — that answer contradicts D-06 and needs `transitions.ts` and `02-CONTEXT.md` amended first, which is a re-plan rather than a task edit.</resume-signal>
</task>

  <action>
Add the two columns and generate the migration with the project's own tooling.

**`src/db/schema.ts`** — add two nullable text columns to the `tasks` table, placed immediately after the
existing `session_id` column so everything session-related sits together:

- `resumedFromTaskId` mapping to `resumed_from_task_id` — the id of the task this one continues, or null for
  an ordinary task. This is the lineage record; it is what makes a resumed run distinguishable from a fresh
  one in the row itself rather than only in the event log.
- `resumeSessionId` mapping to `resume_session_id` — the Claude Code session id this task's spawn should
  continue, or null. Copied from the parent's own `session_id` at resume time.

Give neither a default and add no foreign-key constraint on the lineage column: the existing `project_id`
reference is the only foreign key in this table and adding a self-reference would make the purge path's
delete ordering a new problem for no benefit at single-user scale.

Document in a comment why BOTH columns exist rather than only the lineage one, because the redundancy is
deliberate and a later reader will otherwise "normalise" it away. The lineage column answers "which task did
this continue"; the session column records "which session this run was asked to continue", captured and
validated at resume-request time and therefore independent of whatever later happens to the parent row. The
denormalisation is safe specifically because a parent is terminal before it can be resumed and a terminal
task records no further events, so its `session_id` is immutable — the drift that normally makes a copy
dangerous is unreachable here. Note that plan `02-17`'s dispatch DOES still read the parent row, to derive
the base ref for the resumed worktree from the parent's surviving branch; the session column is an audit
record of the request, not an optimisation that removes that lookup.

**The migration** — run `npm run db:generate -- --name task_resume` so the tool emits
`drizzle/0002_task_resume.sql` and updates the journal and snapshot. Do not hand-write the SQL. Confirm the
generated statements ADD the two columns rather than rebuilding the table — a table rebuild would rewrite
every existing task row, which is a materially different operation from an additive column and is worth
noticing before it ships.

`resume_session_id`, and that each reports as nullable. Assert the journal lists three entries.
  </action>

  <behavior>
    - Resuming a `failed` task that has a session id and a branch name succeeds and returns a NEW task row whose id differs from the parent's.
    - The returned row's lineage column holds the parent's id and its resume-session column holds the parent's session id.
    - The parent row is completely unchanged after the resume — same status, same version, same timestamps.
    - The resumed row inherits the parent's project, title, prompt, model, turn cap, wall-clock cap, and agent profile.
    - Supplying an explicit prompt to the resume overrides the inherited one; omitting it inherits verbatim.
    - Resuming an unknown id raises the not-found code.
    - Resuming a `queued` task raises a distinct not-resumable code whose message names the observed status.
    - Resuming a `running` task raises the same not-resumable code, naming `running`.
    - Resuming a `done`, `approved`, `review`, `needs_human`, or `rejected` task raises the not-resumable code — only the states in the named resumable set are accepted.
    - Resuming a `failed` task whose session id is null raises a distinct no-session code, and creates no row.
    - Resuming a `failed` task whose branch name is null raises a distinct code, and creates no row.
    - Resuming a task at the maximum chain depth raises a distinct depth code; resuming one step below the maximum succeeds.
    - Every refusal leaves the task count unchanged — a rejected resume never half-creates a row.
  </behavior>
  <action>
Write the decision function. Every refusal is a named code, because the failure this closes is a primitive
that existed and was never reached, and the sibling failure is a primitive that is reached and quietly does
something adjacent to what was asked.
